fact: The working paper, from its own interviews, says Zanzibar's CRVS system, which registers births, deaths and marriages, is an outdated system that is difficult to update and relies primarily on paper-based records; it gives no date for the finding, so the paper's date of August 2025 is used.

The Zanzibar Civil Status Registration Agency, established under Act No. 3 of 2018 by merging the Births and Deaths Office with the Registration and Identity Cards Office, registers births, deaths, marriages and divorces with full executive authority in all 11 districts of Zanzibar, as at 2025.

RITA's presentation says e-RITA is a single digital platform that registers all vital events (births, deaths, marriages, divorces and adoptions) and is now the only system used for CRVS, the earlier silo systems having been eliminated; no date is given, so the document's published date is used.

RITA says registration and certification are a one-stop process at local health facilities and community ward executive offices, and that health workers use mobile phones to send birth registration details to a central database, which enables real-time tracking; no date is given, so the document's published date is used.

RITA reports that birth registration points rose from 139 in 2012 to over 12,025 in 2025, in health facilities and ward executive offices, with registration ongoing in all 26 regions; it gives no total of offices and does not say how many of the points enter the record digitally.

RITA presents e-RITA as its own single CRVS platform, run through local government authorities and health facilities, and names the financial and technical sustainability of the CRVS system as a remaining challenge; no date is given, so the document's published date is used.

The Controller and Auditor General states that the Registration Insolvency and Trusteeship Agency (RITA), the statutory registrar of births and deaths, introduced the Civil Registration System in 2017 and runs it, in line with section 19A of Cap. 108 requiring the Registrar General to keep an electronic register of births and deaths.

The audit reports that RITA's Strategic Plan for 2021/22 to 2025/26 names the Civil Registration System as the system to carry out all of RITA's birth and death registration functions, and sets registration targets against it.
The audit's extract of the Civil Registration System shows 18,464,255 births registered and certified as of September 2024 and 977,761 deaths registered cumulatively since the system began in 2017.

The audit found that the 11,053 under-five registration centres (ward offices and health facilities) use both the Civil Registration System and manual registers: registration officers record the birth by hand in the B2 register and then enter the same details into the online system, by phone, which the audit calls double work and partial digitalisation.

RITA officials told the audit that phones given to health centres and Ward Executive Offices to upload registrations performed poorly and were returned without replacement, so certificates were issued at the centre and then taken to district social welfare officers for entry into the system.

The audit states that in October 2024 RITA rolled the Civil Registration System out nationwide to all districts, a rollout that included 11,053 under-five registration centres where both the system and manual registration are used; the share is of districts.

RITA's monitoring and evaluation plan, as the audit reports it, counts 6,341 of 11,053 under-five registration centres as active and 43% as not operating (25% of 3,957 ward centres, 52% of 7,096 health centres), the stated reason being the lack of phones with which a centre uploads registrations; the 57% is active centres, the remainder of the audit's 43%.
The audit records that RITA extended the Civil Registration System to all districts in the country in October 2024.
The audit records that in the 2024/25 financial year RITA received 748 Android phones for uploading registrations, for centres without phones and for new centres.

The audit reports that the Under-Five Birth Registration Initiative, which decentralised registration to 3,957 ward offices and 7,096 health centres in 185 districts, was phased out in 2022/23 after ten years, leaving a backlog of unregistered births, with its sustainability plan still unfinished at the time of the audit.
